v.why: When the learning rate is in the unstable high band, lowering it rescues diverging training and gives large gains (+5 to +50 pp observed), unlike at moderate rates.
Raising an already high learning rate pushes Adam into divergence, causing large accuracy drops (-8 to -34 pp observed).
With very small learning rates the network is undertrained within the epoch budget, so increasing the rate helps more than elsewhere.
Lowering an already tiny learning rate worsens undertraining, so this edit hurts more in the low band than elsewhere.
At large L2 penalties, further increasing alpha over-regularizes the model toward underfitting, giving large drops (-6 to -13 pp observed) instead of the negligible effect seen at small alpha.
Reducing a strong L2 penalty relieves underfitting, whereas at tiny alpha the change is irrelevant.
Shallower networks are far more stable at high learning rates, so removing a layer rescues training (+45 to +50 pp observed on two datasets).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and step count, stabilizing otherwise unstable high-learning-rate training (+13 pp observed on two datasets).
Smaller batches add noise and more updates, amplifying instability when the learning rate is already high.
Wider layers increase the effective step size and instability under a high learning rate, causing large drops (-10 to -27 pp observed) instead of the near-neutral effect at moderate rates.

raw:
These are mostly grounded in the clearest signals from the 100 experiments: the very large effects at high learning rate (0.0774) and at high alpha (0.129 → 1). Where the evidence is thin, I relied on general MLP/Adam training behavior.
